title: the Alvar hymns
hook: a king's wish list: a fish in the temple pond, a tree on the hill, a step at the shrine's door

segments.voice: Yesterday we finished bhakti in the Narada Bhakti Sutras: one love in eleven forms, and its people, among whom there's no distinction, because they are his. Which argument did you skip? Day one thousand two hundred twenty.

A king sits down to write a wish list. He already has the throne, the palace, the treasury, the army. So what does he wish for? To be a fish in a temple pond. A bird by the water. A flowering tree on a hill. And finally, a stone step at the door of a shrine, the kind people walk on without looking down. That king, in Sri Vaishnava tradition, is Kulasekhara, one of the Alvars, and the wish list is one of his hymns. Today, a new block: the Alvar hymns, starting with a king who wanted to be a step.
screen: `A KING'S WISH LIST.` → `A FISH, A BIRD, A TREE.` → `A STEP AT THE SHRINE'S DOOR.`

segments.voice: First, what the Alvar hymns are. The Alvars were poet-saints of Vishnu who sang in Tamil, and the tradition explains their name as people sunk deep in God. Their songs name real temples and real hills, and they speak as servants, lovers, mothers and friends. Year three met two of them, Andal and Nammalvar. Now Kulasekhara. Tradition remembers him as a king of the Chera country, on India's southwest coast, who loved the Lord more than his crown. His hymns are gathered under the name Perumal Tirumozhi, the holy words of the king. In one set of verses he turns toward Venkatam, the sacred hill of Vishnu, and makes his wishes. He doesn't ask to rule the earth, or even the heavens. He asks to be something small on that hill. A bird by the pond there. A fish in its water. A servant who carries things for the Lord. A tree that flowers there. And then the image that stayed. Let me lie as a step, he sings, so I can see your coral mouth. A step at the shrine's door. Stood on by everyone who comes, low and still, but always facing the Lord. The tradition says the threshold step of the shrine at Tirupati, on that hill, carries his name to this day: Kulasekharan padi, Kulasekhara's step. The verses end with something like: let me be anything at all on that hill. Notice what the king is giving up. Not just wealth. Height. Everything in a royal life points upward, and his hymn points down, to the stone under people's feet, because from there you can see the one you love.
screen: `POET-SAINTS OF VISHNU, IN TAMIL.` · `KULASEKHARA, A KING WHO SANG.` · `LET ME LIE AS A STEP.` · `ANYTHING AT ALL ON THAT HILL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the view from the threshold. Sit, and let your gaze drop to the floor a little way in front of you, the height a step would see from. Breathe. Thoughts of rank will come: titles, who's ahead of whom, what you're owed. Let each one pass over you like a footstep, and go on by. Then lift your eyes just a little, toward a picture, a window, or the open space ahead, and keep that one direction, the way the step keeps facing the shrine. If you pray, you can face God this way, from the threshold. The bell holds the time.
The Alvar hymns. Tamil songs to Vishnu by poet-saints the tradition calls sunk deep in God, like Kulasekhara, the king who asked to be a step.
Your line: the Alvar hymns. Today, take the lowest seat once, the back row, the last in line, the one who holds the door, and notice what you can see from there. Day one thousand two hundred twenty.

howItsDone: In Sri Vaishnava worship, the Alvars' Tamil hymns are recited in temples and homes, and pilgrims at Tirupati are told of Kulasekhara Alvar's wish to be a step before the Lord.

trapdoor: what you thought: a king's hymn would ask for power.
what it means: Kulasekhara asks to be a fish, a tree, a step, anything at all on the Lord's hill.
what a scholar hears: the Venkatam decad of the Perumal Tirumozhi, its line about lying as a step to see the coral mouth, and the name Kulasekharan padi kept at the Tirupati shrine's threshold.

notes: First day of the 'Alvar hymns' block (1220–1225). Days 1222 (Tiruppavai), 1223 (the first three Alvars at Tirukkovalur), 1224 (Tiruppallandu) and 1225 (Nammalvar and Nathamuni's recovery of the hymns) were already on disk, so this day takes Kulasekhara and leaves those stories alone. The block's general introduction is kept short for that reason.

The Venkatam decad (Perumal Tirumozhi 4) is paraphrased from memory: the order and exact list of wishes (kurugu bird, fish, servant, champak tree, peak, stream, path, step, anything on the hill) should be checked verse by verse. The 'coral mouth' line (paḍiyāyk kiḍandhu un pavaḷa vāy kāṇbēnē) and 'anything at all on the hill' (ēdēnum āvēnē) are paraphrased; confirm.
'He doesn't ask to rule the earth, or even the heavens' summarizes the decad's refusal of kingship and heavenly rule; confirm against the text.
Kulasekhara as a king of the Chera country and the naming of the Tirupati threshold step (Kulasekharan padi) are stated as tradition; confirm.
'The tradition explains their name as people sunk deep in God' repeats day 907's gloss of āḻvār; a traditional explanation, not a lexicon etymology.
'Perumal Tirumozhi, the holy words of the king': perumāḷ is also a title of the Lord; the rendering follows the usual reading that it names Kulasekhara (Kulasekhara Perumal). Confirm.
Tamil படி: confirm spelling and pronunciation guide.
